results.note: All numbers match 3.1 (pp. 2-3). Results give 8 taking more than labelled (abstract: 7). Results call the 26 loperamide toxicity though 6 were asymptomatic; 'coded as loperamide exposure' follows the Methods.

results.corrected_extracted: Prolonged QTc in 10 of 26 (38.5%), 5 of whom had ventricular dysrhythmias; 9 of the 10 coded misuse (one aged 17) and 1 self-harm; 5 of the 6 with ventricular dysrhythmias had taken loperamide alone, and all but one of the 6 had prolonged QTc (566-749 ms); everyone with a ventricular dysrhythmia whose amount was recorded had taken far more than the label maximum; prolonged QRS in 6 (23.1%); first-degree AV block in 2; myocardial injury and infarction in 1 (3.8%); no reported deaths.
results.note: Numbers right. All but one refers to the 6 with ventricular dysrhythmias (5 had prolonged QTc, matching 5 of 10); now explicit. Paper says 'no reported deaths'. Label maximum is stated in the Discussion (p. 4).
Every Table 5 value matches the rendered p. 4; respiratory depression is printed 15.4% for 5 of 26, and the editors' 19.2% is right.
All counts and percentages match 3.3 (pp. 3-4); benzodiazepines (3, 11%) are left out under 'including', which is fine.

results.corrected_extracted: Only patients seen at the bedside by medical toxicologists, so severity is likely overestimated and the cases likely do not represent exposures that were not hospitalised or had few symptoms; voluntary reporting; ECGs not reviewed by the authors and the QT correction method unknown; exposure not confirmed in biological samples in the vast majority of cases.
results.note: The paper says such exposures are likely not represented, not that they are missed; the series itself includes 6 asymptomatic patients. Also listed there: unblinded authors and treatment decided by primary teams.
Matches the abstract. It also differs from the Results on doses above the label (7 vs 8) and on the search start (November 2011 vs January 2010 in Methods).
Matches the first paragraph of 2.1 (the list is introduced as information including these items); no withdrawal-relief item is described there or in Tables 1-2.
Six misuse cases were attempting to avoid opioid withdrawal; only their reported amounts are given separately, with no treatments or outcomes for the group.
7th Discussion paragraph (p. 5) matches: the behaviour 'may be worsened by' a lack of methadone or buprenorphine programmes, not known in this study.

All values match p. 12; 2784/5390 = 51.65%, so 51.7% is right. Table 2 per-drug totals sum to 8767, not 8881: the gap of 114 equals Table 1 alvimopan trials (1693) minus the alvimopan analysis (1579).
All RRs, CIs, placebo risks and grades match the rendered Table 2. Not listed: prucalopride graded high (one trial), axelopran moderate. HIGH rows carry a three-of-four symbol (printing slip).
Matches the sentence that ends the 2nd paragraph, on p. 12.

results.corrected_extracted: 23 trials: at least one new adverse event 58.2% on drug against 53.0% on placebo, RR 1.10 (1.05-1.16); diarrhoea (22 trials) 8.5% against 4.7%; abdominal pain (22 trials) 12.8% against 5.5%; nausea and/or vomiting (19 trials) 11.5% against 10.1%; dropout for adverse events (20 trials) 7.4% against 4.7%, p = .002, NNH 36 (22-96).
results.note: Added the trial counts (22, 22, 19) for the three side effects. Placebo diarrhoea 147/3182 is 4.6% (printed 4.7%). The table's ratios for these three (1.04, 1.07, 1.03) do not match the rates (crude 1.8, 2.3, 1.1).
Minus signs on Z = -5.06 and -4.79 checked on the rendered p. 11; Q(26) = 105.0 and I2 = 77.9% match; the outlier was 11 of 11 against 0 of 11.

results.corrected_extracted: Patient A, reported as not stopping, had acuity 0.2 in both eyes at presentation and at 40-42 months; patient B improved from 0.2 and 0.5 to −0.1 at 46-48 months with no mention of stopping, which the authors take as a sign that patient B had stopped. Some earlier reports found no improvement in acuity and no resolution of foveal damage within 3 months of presentation despite stopping.
results.note: Patient B's sex is not given, so 'he' is replaced. The studies cited (refs 10 and 35) are a case series and a case report, not both series. The −0.1 was checked on the rendered p. 7.
Matches p. 5. Left out: 8 of 9 followed for more than 3 months (probably more than 6; the subgroups add to 41, not the stated 49). Nothing is reported by whether people stopped.

plain.fix: but: These were only people seen by poisons doctors, who tend to see the sicker cases, and there was no group to compare with, so the study cannot show how often this happens. | how 1: Doctors who treat poisonings in the USA described 26 people seen after taking loperamide; 20 of them had symptoms. | how 3: About 4 in 10 had a change on their heart tracing that can lead to a dangerous heartbeat; some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker, and no deaths were reported. | how 4: Where the amount was recorded, the people with these heart problems had taken far more than the packet says.
plain.note: 6 of 26 had no symptoms; 'nobody knows' goes beyond one study; deaths were not reported rather than ruled out; amounts were recorded for only 9 people. Prolonged QTc is an ECG change, not a rhythm.

plain.fix: short: We can't say yet: the one study we read only described people seen by poisons doctors after taking it. | how 3: The doctors recorded signs of poisoning, such as heart and breathing problems; the study did not report whether the withdrawal eased.
plain.note: Not everyone became ill (6 of 26 had no symptoms), and 'nobody knows' goes beyond the one study. The paper describes no withdrawal-relief item; it does not say one was never written down.

plain.fix: short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, more people's constipation got better. | but: Nearly all the trials were in people taking opioids for pain; only one also included people dependent on opioids, so they say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine treatment. | how 3: In separate trials against a dummy pill, medicines that block opioids in the gut did better than the prescription laxative lubiprostone; no trial compared them directly. | how 4: Diarrhoea and tummy pain were more common on the medicines than on the dummy pill, and slightly more people stopped them because of side effects (about 7 in 100 against 5 in 100).
plain.note: Response was defined in many ways, so 'normally again' overstates. Paulson 2005 enrolled people with opioid dependence, and methadone was among the pain opioids. The drug-class comparison was indirect. Optional: 'dummy treatment', since several methylnaltrexone trials used injections.

plain.fix: but: Its authors say the studies of these laxatives are hard to judge, and we have not read those studies yet.
plain.note: The paper does not call them older. How 1 can stand, though axelopran was an unapproved trial drug; 'newer medicines, none sold in shops' would be exact.

plain.fix: short: In one small study, their methadone level tended to drop faster after its daily high point. | but: Only 18 people were tested for one day, and by our check the difference fell just short of statistical significance, even after the authors left two people out. | how 3: On average, in both groups, withdrawal was lowest in the hours after the dose and grew as the level fell.
plain.note: P = .09 in all 18; the stated P < .05 after leaving two out recomputes to .054. The withdrawal model fitted only 9 of 18 people, so 'in everyone' overstates.

plain.fix: short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye. | but: These are uncontrolled reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot prove poppers were the cause, or show how often it happens or which poppers do it. | how 1: Doctors in at least 12 countries have written about 113 people with eye problems after poppers, some after using them once. | how 3: In most people scanned, the scans showed damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina, at the back of the eye. | how 4: Of the people who had a second scan, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing.
plain.note: The authors say the findings suggest poppers can cause this, and that uncontrolled reports allow no robust associations; bright-light damage looks similar. Some reports are by emergency, toxicology or neurology doctors. Table 1 sums to 116. The follow-up outcome is scans, not vision.

plain.fix: short: We can't say yet: people were told to stop, but no study compared them with people who kept using. | how 1: Where treatment was recorded, doctors told almost all of them to stop using poppers. | how 4: One person who kept using stayed the same, and one whose stopping was not recorded got better.
plain.note: Advice to stop was documented for 42 of 113 (42 of the 45 with treatment recorded), not most people. The sex of patients A and B is not given. 'Nobody knows' goes beyond the review.

lee_2019.funding: Paraphrase of p. 5 Disclosure statement: no specific grant from any public, commercial or not-for-profit funder.
lee_2019.interests: Same statement: no potential conflict of interest and no relevant financial relationships reported.
lee_2019.reporting_errors: Abstract differs from Results: 7 vs 6 ventricular dysrhythmias; QTc cases by intent 6 + 1 vs 9 + 1; 7 vs 8 taking more than labelled; search start November 2011 vs January 2010. Respiratory depression 5 of 26 printed 15.4% (19.2%). Results call all 26 'toxicity' though 6 were asymptomatic.

nee_2018.interests: PDF p. 3 (paraphrase): the authors report no relevant conflicts of interest.
nee_2018.reporting_errors: Accepted manuscript, not the published version. Overall 5390 + 3491 = 8881 exceeds the Table 2 per-drug totals (8767) by 114, exactly Table 1's alvimopan trials (1693) minus the alvimopan analysis (1579). Methylnaltrexone text total 1,619 vs 1,004 + 618 = 1,622 (Table 2: 1622). 2784/5390 printed 51.3% (51.7%). Side-effect table: the 'RR (log)' values for diarrhoea, abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting (1.04, 1.07, 1.03) do not match the event rates (crude 1.81, 2.33, 1.14; they look like 1 + risk difference); abdominal-pain NNH CI 12.3-16.4 ends at the estimate; any-event NNH 21 (text p. 17), 20 (Discussion), 20.6 (table); placebo diarrhoea 4.6% printed 4.7%. HIGH GRADE rows carry three-of-four symbols.

dyer_1999.funding: p. 685 footnote (paraphrase): Royal Adelaide Hospital Research Committee; author scholarships from the Royal Adelaide Hospital (Dawes), the NHMRC (Dora Lush) and the National Drug Strategy.
dyer_1999.reporting_errors: Key P: t = 2.10 after excluding two holders is stated P < .05 but is .054 on 14 df; the printed means and SDs give t = 1.92 (P = .075) or Welch 2.08 (P = .059). Figure 3 legend P < .001 for r = 0.60 vs text P < .01 (recomputed .0085); r = 0.67 stated P < .001 recomputes to .0045. Figure 3's x-axis (0-40 ng/mL/h) cannot hold the group means 47.6 and 74.5. Table I all-patient ± values behave like SEs though labelled SD; peak-to-trough ±0.1 is inconsistent with P > .05 if an SD. The Discussion's split-dose recommendation was not tested in the study.

bartolo_2023.funding: p. 8 Funding (paraphrase): the authors report no funding for this work.
bartolo_2023.interests: p. 8 Disclosure statement (paraphrase): no potential conflict of interest reported.
bartolo_2023.reporting_errors: Table 1 rows add to 116 participants (110 male, 6 female) vs 113 (108/5) in the text, and its ages reach 70 vs the text's range 13-64. Compliance 27 printed as 15% (27/113 = 24%). Four people with three complaints printed 35.7% (7.1%). The 'greater than 3 months' OCT subgroup is probably more than 6 months, and the subgroups add to 41, not 49. The paper calls poppers alkyl nitrates throughout (they are alkyl nitrites). The PDF is the online-first 2022 version.
